issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may determine the nature of a tenancy when that determination is based on proved or admitted facts, including where material documentary evidence was overlooked or factual assumptions were made below.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the original tenants held only a fisheries right, but did not consider material documentary evidence and made factual assumptions.
The High Court considered the evidence and determined the nature of the tenancy from the proved and admitted facts.
The challenge to the High Court’s determination was made in an appeal from its second-appellate judgment.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and sustained the High Court’s determination of the nature of the tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not preclude a High Court in second appeal from determining the nature of a tenancy on proved or admitted facts. The Court also noted that the High Court had identified material documentary evidence overlooked by the first appellate court and factual assumptions in its decision. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged determination was made by a High Court hearing a second appeal.
predicates.material_documents_overlooked: The lower appellate court failed to consider material documentary evidence bearing on the tenancy.
predicates.factual_assumptions_below: The lower appellate court made factual assumptions in deciding the nature of the tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_nature_determinable_from_proved_: The nature of the tenancy could be determined from facts that were proved or admitted.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns the nature of a tenancy and material evidence was overlooked, factual assumptions were made, or the nature can be determined from proved facts, the second-appellate determination is permissible.

issues.legal_issue: A permanent tenancy governed by statutory rules of termination is not ended by a notice that is not shown to satisfy those rules, and an unraised claim of surrender requiring factual inquiry cannot establish termination at a later appellate stage.
material_facts: The High Court found that the tenancy was governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act and had become permanent after twelve years from 1322 B.S.
The plaintiff claimed through a purchase of the original tenants’ rights.
The appellants relied on a notice to quit, but did not show that it complied with the statutory requirements for ending the permanent tenancy.

The appellants also relied on surrender under Section 86 of the Act, but surrender had not been put in issue at trial or pressed before the High Court, and its determination required further examination and investigation.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the notice was not shown to have ended the permanent tenancy and that the surrender argument could not be examined at that stage; the appeal was dismissed and the decree in the plaintiff’s favour stood.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Bengal Tenancy Act, a tenancy governed by the Act and made permanent under its provisions could be terminated only in the manner provided by the Act. The appellants did not establish that the notice complied with those requirements. Although Section 86 provided for surrender, that issue had not been raised below and required factual examination and investigation that could not be undertaken at that stage. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: title_suit_through_tenant and permanent_tenancy and tenancy_governed_by_statutory_termination_rules and notice_compliance_unproven and later_appellate_stage and (surrender_not_raised_below or surrender_requires_further_inquiry)

predicates.title_suit_through_tenant: A claimant seeks title to property through rights acquired from a tenant.
predicates.permanent_tenancy: The tenancy had become permanent under the applicable law.
predicates.tenancy_governed_by_statutory_terminatio: The tenancy was subject to legal rules prescribing how it could be terminated.
predicates.notice_compliance_unproven: The party relying on a termination notice did not establish that it met the applicable legal requirements.
predicates.later_appellate_stage: The claim of termination is being considered at a later stage of appeal.
predicates.surrender_not_raised_below: The party relying on surrender did not put that issue in dispute before the lower courts.
predicates.surrender_requires_further_inquiry: Determining whether surrender occurred requires further factual examination and investigation.

issues.definition: When a claimant relies on a tenant’s rights in a title suit, the tenancy is permanent and governed by statutory termination rules, compliance with a notice is unproven, and a surrender claim was not raised below or requires further inquiry at a later appellate stage, termination of the permanent tenancy is not established.
